does: Stirs dry orzo in hot oil in the pan it will cook in, until the grains turn a pale gold and smell nutty, before any liquid goes in. The grains then keep their shape and give a deeper taste to the dish.

intro.what: Dry orzo is stirred in hot oil until pale gold before the liquid is added.
intro.why: Toasting gives the pasta a nutty taste and helps the grains stay separate in a creamy dish.

how: Soften the onion and garlic in oil first in a wide pan.
Tip in the dry orzo and stir over a medium heat so that every grain is coated.
Keep stirring until the grains turn pale gold and smell nutty, then add the liquid at once.

cues.text: The grains turn from cream to pale gold.
A nutty smell like toasted bread rises from the pan.

mistakes.mistake: Leaving the pan alone, so that the grains on the bottom scorch.
mistakes.fix: Stir all the time while the orzo toasts.

mistakes.mistake: Taking it to dark brown, so the dish tastes bitter.
mistakes.fix: Stop at pale gold and add the liquid.

quiz.question: When is the orzo toasted enough?
choices: When it is pale gold and smells nutty.
When it is dark brown all over.
As soon as it touches the oil.
quiz.because: Pale gold gives a nutty taste without bitterness.

quiz.question: Why stir the whole time?
choices: So that no grains scorch on the bottom of the pan.
quiz.because: Small grains brown fast where they touch the hot pan.

comes_after.why: The orzo goes into onion that has been softened in oil.

variant_of.differs: The pasta is stirred in hot oil in the pan it will cook in, not dried alone in dry heat, and it is taken only to pale gold.
